doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Advice to young improvisers: rhythm and emotion over notes
summary: She tells students to pick one note and swing it, play an emotion, and avoid constant eighth-note chops.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Well what kind of advice do you give people like that?

Well the young students that are just beginning to improvise I always tell them and I mean this is true for everyone, it’s not just all the notes. Yeah that’s important to know what the chord is and know what scale goes with your chord, and that yes you can play it all in eighth notes and you can probably play it in thirty-second notes really fast up and down, I say but that’s not really a good solo is it? No. So what’s going to make your solo good? I think well certainly concentrating on rhythm for really young players and how © Fillius Jazz Archive -16-

you can pick one note and play it in a really swinging rhythm and that’s going to be a better solo than playing five thousand notes just [scats]. And also trying — I say you can play something totally weird, just think of something emotional. Like think of an emotion and play it through your horn. If you want anger, like I just had one girl on a tenor saxophone trying to play a low B flat. I’m like come on — we were playing a B flat blues — just honk on a B flat, just go hooonk, like as loud as you can for like two measures. And she did it and all her band mates were cheering. Because meanwhile she was trying to play like [scats]. That was her solo before. And I’m like that’s not a solo. I said pick one of those notes and just play it. And that’s just to start a kid out. But I actually think it translates to people that are at a really sophisticated level of technique and harmonic knowledge too. Nobody, really, I mean I fall asleep after like one chorus of being impressed with wow they have amazing chops. Wow listen to that, ooh listen to that harmony. But it’s usually the same rhythm [scats] all like constant eighth notes forever, with wow how impressive your chops are. Then after like the fourth chorus— it’s like when somebody talks in your face like I’m doing to you, nonstop, but with no inflection or anything, just like you know, like nonstop like this forever the same exact timbre to everything. And that’s what some people’s solos start sounding like. Even though what I’m saying might be incredibly brilliant but I’m saying it all exactly the same way. That’s like an analogy that I think applies to a lot of players and myself included sometimes.
